## Statement

Let $c_A:U\to\mathbb R^r$ with $r\ge1$ be $C^2$ on a convex ball about $x$, and assume
$\|D^2c_A(z)[u,v]\|_2\le M\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ throughout that ball. Let
$A=Dc_A(x)$ have smallest singular value at least $s_0>0$, and let $p$ be
small enough that $x+p$ and the correction segment stay in the ball. If
$c_A(x)+Ap=0$ and $w$ is the correction of
[[alg-sqp-second-order-correction]], then
$$\|w\|_2\le\frac{M}{2s_0}\|p\|_2^2, \qquad \|c_A(x+p+w)\|_2=O(\|p\|_2^3)\quad(p\to0).$$
The correction is the unique minimum-norm vector satisfying
$Aw=-c_A(x+p)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The $C^2$ active constraint map, bounded second derivative,
uniform row rank, and a step satisfying the linearized active equations.

[F1] [[alg-sqp-second-order-correction]] sets
$w=-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}c_A(x+p)$ and proves it is the minimum-norm solution of
$Aw=-c_A(x+p)$.

[F2] [[cor-second-order-taylor-expansion-with-the-hessian]] gives the
second-order Taylor expansion with a remainder $o(\|p\|_2^2)$ for $C^2$
maps, componentwise.

[A1] The smallest singular value of $A$ is at least $s_0>0$, the second
derivative bound is $M$, and the trial and correction segments lie in the
convex ball.

## Proof

1.1 Taylor's formula along $x+tp$ and the bound on $D^2c_A$ give $$c_A(x+p)=c_A(x)+Ap+R_p=R_p,\qquad \|R_p\|_2\le\frac M2\|p\|_2^2.$$ Since $\|A^T(AA^T)^{-1}\|_2=1/s_{\min}(A)\le1/s_0$, [F1] yields $\|w\|_2\le M\|p\|_2^2/(2s_0)$ and $c_A(x+p)+Aw=0$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Put $y=x+p$. Taylor expansion at $y$ gives $$c_A(y+w)=c_A(y)+Dc_A(y)w+R_w =\bigl(Dc_A(y)-A\bigr)w+R_w,$$ where $\|Dc_A(y)-A\|_2\le M\|p\|_2$ and $\|R_w\|_2\le M\|w\|_2^2/2$. Therefore $$\|c_A(y+w)\|_2\le M\|p\|_2\|w\|_2+\tfrac M2\|w\|_2^2 \le \frac{M^2}{2s_0}\|p\|_2^3+\frac{M^3}{8s_0^2}\|p\|_2^4,$$ which is $O(\|p\|_2^3)$ for small $p$. The minimum-norm assertion is [F1]. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $x_*$ be a KKT point of a $C^2$ program with active inequality set
$I=I(x_*)$, multiplier $\mu_*=(\nu_*,\lambda_{*,I})$, and active
constraint vector $c=(h,g_I)$. Assume LICQ, strict complementarity
$\lambda_{*,i}>0$ for $i\in I$, and the second-order sufficient condition
$d^TH_*d>0$ for every nonzero $d\in\ker A_*$, where
$A_*=Dc(x_*)$ and $H_*=\nabla^2_{xx}L(x_*,\mu_*)$.

For all sufficiently large fixed $\rho$, the PHR augmented-Lagrangian
multiplier update has a local contraction when each inner minimization is
solved exactly. When $r>0$, the same local multiplier convergence holds for inner
points $\widehat x_k$ with stationarity residuals
$\epsilon_k=\|\nabla_x\mathcal L_\rho(\widehat x_k,\nu_k,\lambda_k)\|_2$
whose sum is sufficiently small, provided each point stays in the local
strongly convex branch. More precisely, there are local radii $\delta_\mu$
and $d_x>0$, a strong-convexity constant $\alpha>0$, and a contraction
factor $q<1$ such that convergence holds whenever
$$\|\mu_0-\mu_*\|_2\le\delta_\mu/2,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^\infty\epsilon_k\le \min\left\{\alpha d_x,\frac{(1-q)\delta_\mu}{2C}\right\},$$
where $C=\rho L_c/\alpha$ and $L_c$ is a Lipschitz constant for $c$ on
the local primal neighborhood. Inactive multipliers are initialized at
zero. If $c$ has zero components, the multiplier update is absent and the
bound involving $C$ is omitted; sufficiently local inner points with
summable residuals converge to $x_*$ by strong convexity.

This is a limit theorem for an infinite sequence of successful inner
returns. The contraction estimates apply to any successful prefix of the
finite-budget procedure; the limit conclusion applies only to an infinite
continuation whose calls continue to return within their finite inner caps.
For that procedure, the residual sequence in this theorem is the reported
$\widehat\epsilon_k$; its input tolerances must be chosen so these reports
satisfy the displayed summability bound.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The $C^2$ program, KKT pair, LICQ, strict complementarity,
positive curvature on $\ker A_*$, fixed $\rho$, and summable inner residuals.

[F1] [[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]] defines
LICQ, KKT stationarity, and the $g\le0$, $\lambda\ge0$ convention.

[F2] [[def-sqp-augmented-lagrangian-equality-and-inequality]] defines the
PHR Lagrangian and projected multiplier update.

[F3] [[thm-euclidean-implicit-function-theorem]] gives a local $C^1$
solution branch for a $C^1$ equation with invertible derivative and the
derivative formula for that branch.

[F4] [[alg-sqp-augmented-lagrangian-multiplier-method]] uses the displayed
inner stationarity residual and projected multiplier update, with finite
inner and outer caps and explicit exhaustion/failure returns.

[A1] LICQ holds; every active inequality multiplier is strictly positive;
the Lagrangian Hessian is positive definite on $\ker A_*$; inactive
multipliers start at zero; and inner points stay in a neighborhood where
the PHR branches used below remain fixed.

[A2] Every inner call in the sequence under consideration returns
successfully within its finite cap with the stated residual; an
inner-budget-exhausted or inner-failure status ends the finite procedure and
is not a convergence step.

## Proof

1.1 Write $A=A_*$, $H=H_*$ and $r=\dim c$. Strict complementarity and continuity give a neighborhood in which every active inequality satisfies $\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)>0$ and every inactive inequality, whose multiplier is initialized at zero, satisfies $\lambda_j+\rho g_j(x)<0$. On this branch, [F2] reduces the $x$-dependent augmented Lagrangian to $$\Phi_\rho(x,\mu)=f(x)+\mu^Tc(x)+\frac\rho2\|c(x)\|_2^2,$$ where $\mu=(\nu,\lambda_I)$. Its gradient vanishes at $(x_*,\mu_*)$. [given, F1, F2, algebra, algebra]

1.2 The $x$-Hessian at the base point is $W_\rho=H+\rho A^TA$. If $r=0$, the assumed condition says $H\succ0$. For $r>0$, choose orthonormal matrices $Z,Y$ spanning $\ker A$ and its orthogonal complement, respectively; then $C_0=AY$ is invertible. In this basis the tangent block is $H_T=Z^THZ\succ0$ when its dimension is positive, the cross blocks are those of $H$, and the normal block is $Y^THY+\rho C_0^TC_0$. Its Schur complement over the tangent block is $D+\rho C_0^TC_0$, where $D=Y^THY-Y^THZ H_T^{-1}Z^THY$; if the tangent block is empty, take $D=Y^THY$. Since $C_0^TC_0\succ0$, this Schur complement is positive definite for sufficiently large $\rho$. Hence $W_\rho\succ0$. [given, algebra, choose]

2.1 If $r>0$, apply [F3] to $G(x,\mu)=\nabla_x\Phi_\rho(x,\mu)=0$. Its $x$ derivative is $W_\rho$, which is invertible by step 1.2, and its $\mu$ derivative is $A^T$. Therefore there is a local $C^1$ branch $x(\mu)$ with $x(\mu_*)=x_*$ and $$Dx(\mu_*)=-W_\rho^{-1}A^T.$$ If $r=0$, the empty-multiplier branch consists of the local minimizer $x_*$. By continuity of the Hessian, after shrinking to a convex neighborhood $\Phi_\rho(\cdot,\mu)$ is uniformly strongly convex there; its stationary branch point is its unique local minimizer. [F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For $r>0$, the exact multiplier map is $T(\mu)=\mu+\rho c(x(\mu))$, so $$DT(\mu_*)=I-\rho A W_\rho^{-1}A^T.$$ In the orthonormal coordinates of step 1.2, block elimination gives $A W_\rho^{-1}A^T=C_0(D+\rho C_0^TC_0)^{-1}C_0^T$ $=(\rho I+E)^{-1}$, where $E=C_0^{-T}DC_0^{-1}$ is symmetric. Thus $DT(\mu_*)=E(\rho I+E)^{-1}$. Its eigenvalues are $e_i/(\rho+e_i)$, which have absolute value less than $1$ for all sufficiently large $\rho$. Continuity of $DT$ then gives a closed multiplier ball on which $T$ is a contraction with some factor $q<1$. For $r=0$ the multiplier update is absent. [step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $\widehat x_k$ be an inner point in the selected branch with residual at most $\epsilon_k$, and let $x(\mu_k)$ be the exact branch minimizer. Strong convexity with constant $\alpha$ gives $$\alpha\|\widehat x_k-x(\mu_k)\|_2^2\le \langle\nabla\Phi_\rho(\widehat x_k,\mu_k)- \nabla\Phi_\rho(x(\mu_k),\mu_k),\widehat x_k-x(\mu_k)\rangle \le\epsilon_k\|\widehat x_k-x(\mu_k)\|_2.$$ After cancellation (with the zero-distance case immediate), $\|\widehat x_k-x(\mu_k)\|_2\le\epsilon_k/\alpha$. The multiplier update is on the same PHR branch, so its difference from $T(\mu_k)$ has norm at most $\rho L_c\epsilon_k/\alpha=C\epsilon_k$. Hence $$\|\mu_{k+1}-\mu_*\|_2\le q\|\mu_k-\mu_*\|_2+C\epsilon_k.$$ The stated sum bound keeps this recurrence inside the multiplier ball and keeps every inner point within the primal branch tube. [A1, A2, F2, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Iterating the inequality gives $$\|\mu_k-\mu_*\|_2\le q^k\|\mu_0-\mu_*\|_2+ C\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^{k-1-j}\epsilon_j.$$ The first term tends to zero. For the sum, any fixed finite prefix tends to zero as $k\to\infty$, while the remaining tail is bounded by $C\sum_{j\ge J}\epsilon_j$, which tends to zero as $J\to\infty$. Therefore $\mu_k\to\mu_*$. Also $\epsilon_k\to0$ because it is summable, so step 4.1 gives $\widehat x_k-x(\mu_k)\to0$ and continuity gives $\widehat x_k\to x_*$. When $r=0$, step 1.2 gives a strongly convex local objective and the same residual estimate directly yields $\widehat x_k\to x_*$. [given, A1, A2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The hypotheses and local restrictions used above are exactly the regularity, branch, residual, and successful-inner-call conditions in the Statement and [A2]. This proves the limit claim for the successful update sequence; a finite dispatch may return a cap or failure status first and no global convergence is asserted. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

## Statement

Under the hypotheses of [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]], let $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. It is a smooth manifold of dimension $d-m$. Choose a local configuration chart $\phi:O\subseteq\mathbb R^{d-m}\to Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and write $T=D\phi$, $G=T^TMT$. The cotangent coordinates $\pi=T^Tp$ identify the part of $\mathcal M$ over this chart locally with $T^*Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$: the unique consistent ambient momentum representing $\pi$ is $p=MTG^{-1}\pi$. In these coordinates the restricted canonical one-form $p^Tdq$ is $\pi^Tdx$, so the restricted two-form is $\omega_{\mathcal M}=\sum_{j=1}^{d-m}dx_j\wedge d\pi_j$. It is closed and nondegenerate, hence is symplectic on the regular phase manifold.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The objects and regularity hypotheses in [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]], and the canonical symplectic convention in [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]].

[F1] [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]]: $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$, $M$ is constant SPD, and $\mathcal M$ consists of $(q,p)$ with $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $JM^{-1}p=0$.

[F2] [[thm-parametrized-implicit-function-theorem-with-higher-regularity]]: if a square block derivative of a $C^k$ map is invertible at a zero, its zero set is locally the graph of a unique $C^k$ function; this applies for every finite $k$ when the map is smooth.

[F3] [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]: a symplectic form is a smooth closed two-form that is pointwise nondegenerate.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composite is the composite of its derivatives.

## Proof

1.1 At any $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, full row rank of $J(q)$ gives a permutation of coordinates $q=(x,y)$ for which the $m\times m$ block $D_yc(q)$ is invertible. Apply [F2] to the smooth map $c$ for each finite $k\ge1$. The resulting local graphs agree with the unique $C^1$ graph on overlaps, so that graph is $C^k$ locally for every $k$ and hence smooth. Thus locally $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is $y=\psi(x)$; $\phi(x)=(x,\psi(x))$ parametrizes it, and $D\phi$ has rank $d-m$ with image $\ker J$. [F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Define $G(x)=D\phi(x)^TMD\phi(x)$. For every nonzero $\xi$, $D\phi\,\xi\ne0$ and $\xi^TG(x)\xi=(D\phi\,\xi)^TM(D\phi\,\xi)>0$, so $G$ is invertible. Its entries are smooth, and $G^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(G)/\det G$ is smooth because $\det G>0$. For a cotangent coordinate $\pi\in\mathbb R^{d-m}$, put $p=MD\phi\,G^{-1}\pi$. Then $JM^{-1}p=JD\phi\,G^{-1}\pi=0$ and $D\phi^Tp=G G^{-1}\pi=\pi$. Conversely, if $JM^{-1}p=0$, then $M^{-1}p=D\phi\,\xi$ for a unique $\xi$, and $D\phi^Tp=G\xi$; hence the displayed formula gives the unique ambient $p$ representing $\pi$. Both this map and its inverse $(q,p)\mapsto(x,D\phi(x)^Tp)$ are smooth, so $(x,\pi)\mapsto(\phi(x),p)$ is a local diffeomorphism from $T^*Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ onto the part of $\mathcal M$ over this chart. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\theta_0=p^Tdq$ be the ambient canonical one-form. Under the chart just constructed, $dq=D\phi\,dx$ and $D\phi^Tp=\pi$, so its pullback is $\pi^Tdx$. Therefore the pullback of $\omega_0=-d\theta_0$ is $\sum_{j=1}^{d-m}dx_j\wedge d\pi_j$, which is closed and nondegenerate. [F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Every point of $\mathcal M$ has a chart of this form; the local calculation proves the restricted two-form is closed and nondegenerate everywhere. By [F3] it is symplectic, as claimed. [F3, step 3.1] ∎

## Definition

The input state is consistent, $(q,p)\in\mathcal M$. For $h=0$, return $(q,p)$ with status `exact-identity`. For nonzero $h$, fix a compact phase subset $C\subset\mathcal M$ over a compact regular configuration chart with $(q,p)\in C$ and $0<|h|<h_0(C)$, using branch balls $U_q,U_p$ supplied by [[lem-rattle-scaled-position-and-momentum-branches]]. The admissible inputs also include initial guesses $\lambda_{\mathrm{init}}\in U_q$, $\mu_{\mathrm{init}}\in U_p$, tolerances $\varepsilon_q,\varepsilon_p\ge0$, finite correction budgets $N_q,N_p\in\mathbb N_0$, and terminating exact factorization/solve backends $\mathcal B_q,\mathcal B_p$ for the two chord calls. Each backend accepts a square $m\times m$ Jacobian, returns a singularity report exactly when it is singular, and otherwise returns a retained factor object. For every right-hand side, solving on this object terminates with the exact unique solution for that matrix; factorization and retained-factor solves are separate operations, as in [[alg-newton-chord-implicit-residual-with-factorization-reuse]]. All evaluations of $c,J,\nabla V$ and the displayed matrix operations in the updates, residual and exact residual-Jacobian evaluations, arithmetic, Euclidean norm evaluation/comparison, and domain-membership tests are returning primitives; no bound on their internal cost is specified. The multiplier domains $U_q,U_p\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ are open balls within the regular branch neighborhoods. Choose the balls so that $F_q$ is $C^1$ on $U_q$ and, for every $\lambda\in U_q$, the corresponding $F_p$ is $C^1$ on $U_p$ and all evaluations in the updates are defined and the corresponding positions remain in the ambient full-row-rank configuration region of the branch lemma. Inconsistent input, missing branch balls, or maps not defined on these domains are outside the algorithm's admissible inputs. On success the routine returns the approximate state, both multipliers, and both scaled residual norms; on failure it returns the residual solver's status, last valid multiplier iterate, and actual scaled residual norm, together with any position-stage values already computed.

1. Form
$$F_q(\lambda)=h^{-2}c\!\left(q+hM^{-1}\left(p-\frac h2\nabla V(q)-hJ(q)^T\lambda\right)\right).$$
Run [[alg-newton-chord-implicit-residual-with-factorization-reuse]] on $F_q$ in chord mode with refresh period $1$, domain $U_q$, initial value $\lambda_{\mathrm{init}}$, tolerance $\varepsilon_q$, budget $N_q$, and backend $\mathcal B_q$. If it returns anything other than `root`, return its exact status (`iteration-budget-exhausted`, `singular-jacobian`, or `invalid-trial`), last valid multiplier iterate, and actual scaled residual norm; do not continue.

2. For its returned $\widetilde\lambda$, compute $\widetilde p_{1/2}=p-\frac h2\nabla V(q)-hJ(q)^T\widetilde\lambda$ and $\widetilde q_1=q+hM^{-1}\widetilde p_{1/2}$. Form
$$F_p(\mu)=h^{-1}J(\widetilde q_1)M^{-1}\left(\widetilde p_{1/2}-\frac h2\nabla V(\widetilde q_1)-hJ(\widetilde q_1)^T\mu\right).$$
Run the same supplier procedure on $F_p$ in chord mode with refresh period $1$, domain $U_p$, initial value $\mu_{\mathrm{init}}$, tolerance $\varepsilon_p$, budget $N_p$, and backend $\mathcal B_p$. If it returns anything other than `root`, return its exact status (`iteration-budget-exhausted`, `singular-jacobian`, or `invalid-trial`), last valid multiplier iterate, actual scaled tangency residual norm, and the successful position-stage values; do not continue.

3. If both calls meet their residual tolerances, set

## Statement

**Given:** The two absolute-convergence assumptions in the Statement.

$$\frac{(c+h)^n-c^n}{h}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(c+h)^{n-1-j}c^j,$$
so every term has modulus at most $R^{n-1}$ and the quotient has modulus at most $nR^{n-1}$. $$m_{\mathrm{tot}}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{J}x_i n_i(t)+L(t)$$

$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+M_h/\alpha_h)\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\alpha_h,$$

where $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)=\sup_{w_h\ne0}|F_h(w_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|/\|w_h\|_h$. The estimate requires the bounded extension and does not assert that every nonconforming, penalty, or discontinuous Galerkin form has one.

## Statement

Let $N\ge2$ and $x_j=2\pi j/N$. If integers $k,r$ satisfy $k\equiv r\pmod N$, then
$$
e^{ikx_j}=e^{irx_j}\qquad(0\le j<N).
$$
Consequently, sampling a product of Fourier modes with frequencies $k_1,\ldots,k_s$ gives the same nodal data as the single mode whose frequency is the sum $\sum_{\ell=1}^s k_\ell$ reduced modulo $N$.

The frequency space in [[def-periodic-fourier-collocation-grid]] is real-valued. For complex data, let $\mathcal T_N^{\mathbb C}$ be the space obtained by allowing complex coefficients in that same real basis, and extend its cardinal formula by
$$
I_N^{\mathbb C}V(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}V_jL_j(x),\qquad V\in\mathbb C^N.
$$
Then $I_N^{\mathbb C}V$ is the unique member of $\mathcal T_N^{\mathbb C}$ with nodal data $V$. On real data this formula agrees with $I_N$; in the even case the complex Nyquist samples are interpolated by the real basis function $\cos(Nx/2)$.

**Given:** An integer $N\ge2$, its periodic grid, and integers $k,r$ with $k-r=qN$ for some integer $q$.

[F2] [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]: $e^{z+w}=e^ze^w$; [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]: $e^w=1$ when $w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$.

[F3] [[lem-orthogonality-of-characters-on-a-finite-cyclic-group]]: the sum over a complete residue system of the characters at $i-j$ is $N$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise.

[F4] [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]]: complex nodal data on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ have a unique finite Fourier representation.

[F5] [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]: $e^{it}=\cos t+i\sin t$ for real $t$.

[F6] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]: $\sin0=0$ and $\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x$, hence $\sin(m\pi)=0$ for every integer $m$.

[F4] [[lem-chebyshev-polynomials-orthogonal-in-arcsine-weight]]: $\|T_0\|_C^2=\pi$ and $\|T_r\|_C^2=\pi/2$ for $r\ge1$, with distinct modes orthogonal.

## Statement

$$
E_\rho=\left\{\frac{\rho e^{it}+\rho^{-1}e^{-it}}2:0\le t\le2\pi\right\}

$$
\|f-I_N^Lf\|_C\le \frac{4\sqrt{\pi}M}{\rho-1}\rho^{-N}.
$$

**Given:** $\rho>1$, a function $f$ holomorphic near $E_\rho$ with $|f|\le M$ there, and $N\ge1$.

[F1] [[thm-cauchy-theorem-one-exceptional-point-on-a-star-shaped-domain]]: a holomorphic function on a star-shaped open set has zero integral around every closed rectifiable contour in that set.

[F2] [[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]] and [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]: $T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta)$ and cosine is even and $2\pi$-periodic.

[F3] [[lem-chebyshev-lobatto-mode-aliasing]]: $I_N^LT_n=T_{\rho_N(n)}$ for the folded degree $0\le\rho_N(n)\le N$.

[F4] [[lem-chebyshev-polynomials-orthogonal-in-arcsine-weight]]: the coefficient convention is $c_0=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)d\theta$, $c_n=2\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\cos(n\theta)d\theta$ for $n\ge1$, and a continuous function with all Chebyshev coefficients zero is zero.

[F5] [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]]: the angular measure has total mass $\pi$, so $\|h\|_C\le\sqrt\pi\|h\|_\infty$.

[F6] [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]]: $|\cos t|\le1$ for real $t$.

[F7] [[thm-geometric-series]]: for $r\in\mathbb R$ with $|r|<1$, $\sum_{k\ge0}r^k=1/(1-r)$.

## Statement

Under the hypotheses of [[def-weighted-orthogonal-polynomial-galerkin-space]], for every real measurable $u$ such that $\int|u p_j|\,d\mu<\infty$ for $0\le j\le N$, the formula
$$
\Pi_Nu=\sum_{j=0}^{N}\frac{\int u(x)p_j(x)\,d\mu(x)}{h_j}\,p_j
$$
is finite and defines the unique element of $V_N(\mu)$ whose residual is orthogonal to every $p_i$, $0\le i\le N$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite positive measure $\mu$ with the support condition in [[def-weighted-orthogonal-polynomial-galerkin-space]], an integer $N\ge0$, and a real measurable $u$ with $\int|u p_j|\,d\mu<\infty$ for $0\le j\le N$.

[F1] [[def-weighted-orthogonal-polynomial-galerkin-space]]: the basis polynomials $p_0,\ldots,p_N$ are monic orthogonal polynomials and $h_j=\int p_j^2\,d\mu>0$.

[F2] [[thm-gauss-polynomial-moment-pairing-is-an-inner-product]]: on each finite polynomial space allowed by the moment data, the moment pairing is a positive-definite real inner product.

[F3] The given integrability hypotheses make each numerator $\int u p_j\,d\mu$ a finite real number.

## Proof

1.1 Each numerator is finite by [F3], and each denominator $h_j$ is finite and strictly positive by [F1]–[F2]. Thus every coefficient in the displayed finite sum is a defined real number. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

Thus $\Pi_Nu\in V_N(\mu)$ has the required residual orthogonality. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $v\in V_N(\mu)$ has the same residual property, then $w=v-\Pi_Nu$ lies in $V_N(\mu)$ and is orthogonal to every basis vector, hence to itself. Positive definiteness in [F2] gives $\int w^2\,d\mu=0$, so $w=0$ in $L^2(\mu)$ and $v=\Pi_Nu$. This proves uniqueness. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$
\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},
\qquad
\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},
$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Nonnegative integers $m,n$ and the Rodrigues polynomials $P_k$.

[F1] [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]]: $P_n=(2^nn!)^{-1}D^n(x^2-1)^n$ and $\langle p,q\rangle_L=\int_{-1}^1pq$.

[F2] [[thm-integration-by-parts]]: for differentiable factors with integrable derivatives on a closed interval, $\int uv'=[uv]-\int u'v$.

[F3] [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]]: $D(x^k)=kx^{k-1}$ for positive integer $k$, and constants differentiate to zero; repeated application gives the derivatives of monomials.

[F4] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: polynomial sums, products, and scalar multiples obey the usual derivative rules.

## Proof

1.1 Write $(x^2-1)^n=(x-1)^n(x+1)^n$. For every $j<n$, its $j$th derivative vanishes at both endpoints: by the product rule, every term differentiates each factor at most $j<n$ times and retains a positive power of the factor that vanishes at that endpoint. Thus $n$ integrations by parts in [F2] give, for every polynomial $q$ of degree less than $n$, $\int_{-1}^1P_nq=\frac{(-1)^n}{2^nn!}\int_{-1}^1(x^2-1)^nq^{(n)}=0,$ because $q^{(n)}=0$ by [F3]. Hence $P_n$ is orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, induction]

2.1 The leading term of $(x^2-1)^n$ is $x^{2n}$; differentiating it $n$ times gives $(2n)!/n!$ times $x^n$ by [F3]. All other terms have lower degree after differentiation. Therefore $P_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $\kappa_n=(2n)!/(2^n(n!)^2)>0$. The distinct degrees imply the family $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ is linearly independent and spans every polynomial of degree at most $N$, by successive elimination of leading terms. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $P_n-\kappa_nx^n$ has degree less than $n$, step 1.1 gives $\int_{-1}^1P_n^2=\kappa_n\int_{-1}^1P_nx^n.$ Apply [F2] $n$ times to the Rodrigues formula against $x^n$. The endpoint terms vanish as in step 1.1 and $(x^n)^{(n)}=n!$, so $\int_{-1}^1P_nx^n=\frac1{2^n}\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^n\,dx.$ [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Put $J_n=\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^n dx$. Then $J_0=2$. For $n\ge1$, the endpoint values of $x(1-x^2)^n$ are zero, so integrating its derivative gives $0=J_n-2n(J_{n-1}-J_n),\qquad J_n=\frac{2n}{2n+1}J_{n-1}.$ Induction yields $J_n=2^{2n+1}(n!)^2/(2n+1)!$. Substituting this and $\kappa_n$ from step 2.1 into step 3.1 gives $\int P_n^2=2/(2n+1)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the first orthogonality formula, including $n=0$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, induction, algebra]

5.1 When $n=0$, $P_0=1$ and $Q_0=-((1-x^2)P_0')'=0$, so $Q_0=0\cdot P_0$. Now take $n\ge1$ and define $Q_n=-((1-x^2)P_n')'$. Its leading term is $n(n+1)\kappa_nx^n$, so $Q_n-n(n+1)P_n$ has degree less than $n$. For any polynomial $q$ of degree less than $n$, two integrations by parts give $\int_{-1}^1Q_nq=\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'q'=-\int_{-1}^1P_n((1-x^2)q')'=0,$ where both boundary terms vanish because of the factor $1-x^2$, and the last polynomial paired with $P_n$ has degree less than $n$, so step 1.1 applies. Therefore $Q_n-n(n+1)P_n$ is a lower-degree polynomial orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial. Expand it in the basis from step 2.1; the first formula and the positive norms in step 4.1 force every coefficient to be zero. Thus $Q_n=n(n+1)P_n$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 One integration by parts and step 5.1 give $\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'P_m'=\int_{-1}^1Q_nP_m=n(n+1)\int_{-1}^1P_nP_m.$ The first formula, already proved in step 4.1 and step 1.1, yields the displayed weighted derivative identity for every $m,n\ge0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $s\ge0$, $N\ge0$, and $u=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nP_n\in H_L^s$ from [[def-legendre-weighted-sobolev-scale]]. Then
$$
\|u-\Pi_Nu\|_{L_L^2}\le(1+(N+1)(N+2))^{-s/2}\|u\|_{H_L^s}.

## Definition

Let $U,V,a,b$ satisfy [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]]. **Inputs:** an integer $M\ge2$, images $R_0=a,R_1,\ldots,R_{M-1},R_M=b$ in $U$, a step size $\eta>0$, force and spacing tolerances $\tau_F,\tau_s\ge0$, and a finite update budget $N\in\mathbb N_0$. **Output:** the last image chain and one of `tolerances-met`, `geometry-failure`, `nonfinite-evaluation`, or `budget-exhausted`. A stop status is an algorithmic report, not a continuum-error certificate.

At iteration $k=0,\ldots,N$, perform the following in order.

1. For each interior $i=1,\ldots,M-1$, form the centered chord $c_i=R_{i+1}-R_{i-1}$. If $c_i=0$, return `geometry-failure`. Otherwise put $t_i=c_i/\|c_i\|_2$ and $F_i^\perp=-(I-t_it_i^T)\nabla V(R_i)$. If any force is nonfinite, return `nonfinite-evaluation`.
2. For the current chain set $\ell_i=\|R_i-R_{i-1}\|_2$ for $1\le i\le M$, $\bar\ell=M^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^M\ell_i$, $r_F=\max_{1\le i<M}\|F_i^\perp\|_2$, and $r_s=\max_{1\le i\le M}|\ell_i-\bar\ell|$. If $r_F\le\tau_F$ and $r_s\le\tau_s$, return `tolerances-met`.
3. If $k=N$, return `budget-exhausted`. Otherwise set $Y_0=a$, $Y_M=b$, and $Y_i=R_i+\eta F_i^\perp$ for interior images. Reject any nonfinite $Y_i$ with `nonfinite-evaluation`; if any $Y_i\notin U$, return `geometry-failure`.
4. Compute cumulative lengths $s_0=0$, $s_j=\sum_{i=1}^j\|Y_i-Y_{i-1}\|_2$, and total length $S=s_M$. If $S=0$ or any segment length is zero, return `geometry-failure`. For $j=1,\ldots,M-1$, place the new image at the unique point of the piecewise-linear polygon $Y_0,\ldots,Y_M$ whose cumulative length is $jS/M$; if that target is a vertex, use that vertex, and otherwise use linear interpolation on its unique containing segment. If any redistributed image lies outside $U$, return `geometry-failure`. Set $R_0^{k+1}=a,R_M^{k+1}=b$ and use the checked redistributed points as the new interior images.

This is the specified projected-force string variant. No convergence from arbitrary initial images, no automatic endpoint minimization, and no error estimate follow from the procedure alone.

## Statement

For $0\prec D\prec I$ and every Hermitian direction $H$, let
$\mathcal S(D)=\operatorname{tr}(D\log D+(I-D)\log(I-D))$. Then
$$D\mathcal S(D)[H]=\operatorname{tr}\big(H(\log D-\log(I-D))\big).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive-definite Hermitian matrices $D$ and $I-D$, the spectral definition of matrix logarithm, and the real Fréchet derivative on $\mathbb H_n$.

[F1] For $x>0$, $\log x=\int_0^\infty((1+s)^{-1}-(x+s)^{-1})\,ds$ and $\log'(x)=1/x$ ([[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]).

[F2] Matrix inversion is differentiable with $D\operatorname{inv}(A)[H]=-A^{-1}HA^{-1}$ ([[thm-derivative-of-matrix-inversion]]).

[F3] Trace and Frobenius-linear matrix functionals differentiate by their linear increments ([[prop-differentials-of-trace-and-frobenius-linear-functionals]]).

[F4] A finite-dimensional complex Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis and its scalar functional calculus is defined on its spectrum ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]], [[def-functional-calculus-for-a-normal-endomorphism]]).

[F5] Matrix differentials obey the product rule ([[prop-matrix-differentials-obey-sum-product-and-adjoint-rules]]).

## Proof


1.1 For positive scalars the integral in [F1] converges and equals $\log x$ by integrating over $[0,R]$ and taking $R\to\infty$. Diagonalizing a positive-definite Hermitian $X$ by [F4] gives the same identity for $\log X$. If $X\succeq mI$ for some $m>0$, the resolvent $R_s=(X+sI)^{-1}$ has norm at most $(m+s)^{-1}$. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 In the neighborhood $X\succeq (m/2)I$, the resolvent identity gives $\frac{R_s(X+tH)-R_s(X)}{t}=-R_s(X+tH)H R_s(X)$. On every bounded interval of $s$, [F2] and continuity give uniform convergence of these difference quotients to $-R_sHR_s$. For $s\ge R\ge1$, their norm is at most $\|H\|_2/s^2$, so the integral of the tail is at most $\|H\|_2/R$, uniformly for small $t$. First differentiating on $[0,R]$ and then letting $R\to\infty$ proves $D\log(X)[H]=\int_0^\infty R_sHR_s\,ds$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given]

3.1 By the product rule [F5] and trace differential [F3], $D\operatorname{tr}(X\log X)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(H\log X)+\int_0^\infty\operatorname{tr}(XR_sHR_s)\,ds$. The trace identity $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ follows by expanding the diagonal sums. Since $X$ commutes with $R_s$, it rewrites the integral as $\operatorname{tr}(H\int_0^\infty XR_s^2\,ds)$. Diagonalizing $X$ and using $\int_0^\infty x(x+s)^{-2}\,ds=1$ for each eigenvalue $x>0$ makes the matrix integral $I$. Thus $D\operatorname{tr}(X\log X)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(H(\log X+I))$. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply step 3.1 first with $X=D$ and direction $H$, then with $X=I-D$ and direction $-H$. The identity terms cancel, leaving $D\mathcal S(D)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(H(\log D-\log(I-D)))$. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the data of [[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]], $E(P)$ is real
and $C^2$ on its stated neighborhood. For every Hermitian $P$ in that
neighborhood and every Hermitian direction $H$,
$$DE(P)[H]=\operatorname{tr}\big((h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P))H\big)=\langle F(P),H\rangle_F.$$
Thus $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius gradient of $E$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Hermitian $h,P,H$, a real-linear self-adjoint map $G$ on $\mathbb H_n$, and a real $C^2$ functional $E_{xc}$ on an open neighborhood of $P$.

[F1] Trace and Frobenius-linear functionals differentiate by their linear increments ([[prop-differentials-of-trace-and-frobenius-linear-functionals]]).

[F2] Matrix differentials obey the sum, product, and adjoint rules ([[prop-matrix-differentials-obey-sum-product-and-adjoint-rules]]).

[F3] In the projector energy model, $G$ is real-linear and self-adjoint and $E_{xc}$ has its Frobenius gradient ([[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]]).

[F4] For conformable matrices over a field, $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ ([[thm-trace-of-ab-equals-trace-of-ba]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $A,B$ are Hermitian, then $\overline{\operatorname{tr}(AB)}=\operatorname{tr}((AB)^*)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ by the trace identity [F4]. Hence $\operatorname{tr}(hP)$ and $\operatorname{tr}(P G(P))$ are real; $E_{xc}$ is real by [F3]. The first two terms are polynomial in the real coordinates of $P$, so together with the $C^2$ term they give a real $C^2$ function. [F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 For real $t$, real-linearity gives $G(P+tH)=G(P)+tG(H)$. Expanding and collecting the coefficient of $t$ yields $\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}((P+tH)G(P+tH))=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(H G(P)) +\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(H))$. The linear trace term differentiates to $\operatorname{tr}(hH)$ by [F1], and the $E_{xc}$ term differentiates to $\langle\nabla E_{xc}(P),H\rangle_F$ by its gradient definition. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Self-adjointness of $G$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(P G(H))=\langle P,G(H)\rangle_F=\langle G(P),H\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(G(P)H)$. Since these traces are real, the two quadratic contributions in step 1.2 combine to $\operatorname{tr}(G(P)H)$. Adding the other derivatives gives $DE(P)[H]=\langle h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P),H\rangle_F$. This is the unique Frobenius gradient pairing, so it equals $\langle F(P),H\rangle_F$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $D$ be a global minimizer of $\mathcal F_\beta$ from
[[def-finite-temperature-density-matrix-free-energy]]. It is interior by
[[lem-finite-temperature-minimizer-is-interior]]. If
$F_{\mathcal E}(D)=\nabla\mathcal E(D)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius gradient of
the energy, then there is a real chemical potential $\mu$ such that
$$D=\bigl(I+\exp(\beta(F_{\mathcal E}(D)-\mu I))\bigr)^{-1}.$$
For a fixed Hermitian field $F$ independent of $D$, the equation
$$\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{1}{1+\exp(\beta(\lambda_j(F)-\mu))}=r$$
has exactly one real solution $\mu$ when $0<r<n$. In a nonlinear
self-consistent model, this uniqueness of $\mu$ for each fixed field does not
imply uniqueness of the density solving the self-consistency equation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge2$, $0<r<n$, $\beta>0$, a real $C^1$ energy $\mathcal E$, and an interior minimizer $D$ of its entropy-regularized free energy.

[F1] The trace-constrained density domain and free-energy functional are as in the finite-temperature definition ([[def-finite-temperature-density-matrix-free-energy]]).

[F2] Every minimizer has $0\prec D\prec I$ ([[lem-finite-temperature-minimizer-is-interior]]).

[F3] For interior $D$, the entropy trace derivative is $\operatorname{tr}(H(\log D-\log(I-D)))$ ([[prop-interior-entropy-trace-derivative]]).

[F4] A finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis and its scalar functions act on eigenvalues ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]], [[prop-functional-calculus-for-normal-endomorphisms]]).

[F5] A continuous real function on an interval takes every value between its endpoint values ([[thm-intermediate-value]]).

[F6] The real exponential is continuous and strictly increasing, tends to $0$ at $-\infty$ and to $+\infty$ at $+\infty$, and takes only positive values ([[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]]).

## Proof


1.1 Let $H$ be any traceless Hermitian matrix. Since $D$ and $I-D$ are positive definite, their least eigenvalues have a positive minimum $\delta$. For $|t|\|H\|_2<\delta$, both $D+tH$ and $I-D-tH$ remain positive definite, and the trace remains $r$. Thus $D+tH$ is feasible for both signs of small $t$. At a minimizer its directional derivative is zero; [F3] gives
$$\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\left[F_{\mathcal E}(D)+\beta^{-1}(\log D-\log(I-D))\right]H\right)=0.$$
[F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 Put $A=F_{\mathcal E}(D)+\beta^{-1}(\log D-\log(I-D))$. This is Hermitian. Choose $H=A-(\operatorname{tr}A/n)I$, which is Hermitian and traceless. Step 1.1 gives $0=\operatorname{tr}(AH)=\operatorname{tr}(H^2)=\|H\|_F^2$, hence $H=0$ and $A=\mu I$ with real $\mu=\operatorname{tr}A/n$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Rearranging step 2.1 gives $F_{\mathcal E}(D)=\mu I-\beta^{-1}(\log D-\log(I-D))$, so $F_{\mathcal E}(D)$ is a scalar function of $D$. In the spectral basis of $D$, for each eigenvalue $d\in(0,1)$ the scalar equation is $\lambda=\mu-\beta^{-1}\log(d/(1-d))$, whose unique solution is $d=(1+\exp(\beta(\lambda-\mu)))^{-1}$. Applying this scalar identity to the spectral functional calculus [F4] proves the matrix formula. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For a fixed Hermitian $F$, diagonalize it by [F4] with real eigenvalues $\lambda_j(F)$, and define $g(\mu):=\sum_{j=1}^n(1+\exp(\beta(\lambda_j(F)-\mu)))^{-1}$. By [F6] and $\beta>0$, each summand is continuous and strictly increasing in $\mu$. Its limits are $0$ as $\mu\to-\infty$ and $1$ as $\mu\to+\infty$, so $g$ is continuous and strictly increasing with limits $0$ and $n$. Since $0<r<n$, these limits give finite real numbers $\mu_-$ and $\mu_+$ with $g(\mu_-)<r<g(\mu_+)$. Strict increase implies $\mu_-<\mu_+$. Applying [F5] to $g$ on the closed interval $[\mu_-,\mu_+]$ gives a solution with $g(\mu)=r$, and strict increase makes it unique. This scalar argument proves uniqueness of the multiplier for the fixed field only. [F4, F5, F6, given, choose, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $Q:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a finite quadrature functional of the form
$$Q(g)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i g(x_i),$$
where $m\ge1$, the nodes $x_i\in[0,1]$ are distinct, and $w_i\in\mathbb R$.
A one-dimensional **nested level hierarchy** is a sequence
$(Q_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0}$ of such functionals, with node sets
$X_\ell=\{x_{\ell,i}:1\le i\le m_\ell\}$ satisfying
$X_{\ell-1}\subseteq X_\ell$ for every $\ell\ge1$.
Set $Q_{-1}:=0$, the zero functional, and define the **detail functional**
$$\Delta_0:=Q_0,\qquad \Delta_\ell:=Q_\ell-Q_{\ell-1}\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
Finite sums are as in [[def-finite-sum]]. For each $d\ge1$, the integration
functional used below is $I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f$, with the multiple Riemann
integral convention of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]].

The convergence and rate results in this pair use the **dyadic composite-
Simpson hierarchy**
$$Q_\ell(g):=Q_S(g;0,1,2^{\ell+1}),\qquad X_\ell=\{k/2^{\ell+1}:0\le k\le2^{\ell+1}\},$$
where $Q_S$ is the even-panel rule of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. The
number of panels is even and at least two. The sets are nested because
$k/2^{\ell}=2k/2^{\ell+1}$, and their weights are nonnegative with total
weight one: each two-panel block has nonnegative weights $H(1,4,1)/6$
summing to its length $H$, and the blocks partition an interval of length one.
Level zero has nodes $0,1/2,1$ and weights $1/6,4/6,1/6$.

For a multi-index $\ell=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, any tensor
product $R_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes R_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$ of these
finite functionals means the finite weighted functional obtained by multiplying
the coordinate weights and evaluating on the corresponding node tuples. In
particular, $\Delta_\ell:=\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes
\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$. No exactness or error property is implied by the
notation alone.

## Definition

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$. A finite set $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ is
**downward closed** if, whenever $\ell\in\Lambda$ and $\ell_j>0$, the index
$\ell-e_j$ also belongs to $\Lambda$; here $e_j$ is the $j$th coordinate unit
vector. In this pair an admissible Smolyak set is a nonempty finite downward-
closed $\Lambda$ that contains $0$.

For a level hierarchy from [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]], define
the **Smolyak cubature functional**
$$Q_\Lambda(f):=\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Each summand is a finite signed weighted sum. Expanding all differences and
adding coefficients at equal points gives one finite signed weight for each
distinct node in
$$\mathcal N_\Lambda:=\bigcup_{\ell\in\Lambda}X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}.$$
The **node-union work count** for this direct evaluation convention is
$W(\Lambda):=|\mathcal N_\Lambda|$, so shared nodes are counted once. A
combined weight may be negative or zero; no positivity claim follows from the
definition.

## Definition

**Input:** dimension $d\ge1$, a finite downward-closed $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb
N_0^d$ containing $0$, the finitely many levels required by $\Lambda$, a
function $f$ evaluable at their nodes, and for each exact node a canonical key
in a totally ordered set. Keys must agree exactly if and only if the real node
tuples agree. If any required rule or key is missing, return `invalid-input`.

**Output:** the sorted list of distinct node tuples with their combined signed
weights, the value $Q_\Lambda(f)$, and the actual evaluation count
$W(\Lambda)$.

1. Expand each detail $\Delta_\ell$ in the finite Smolyak sum of
   [[def-smolyak-cubature]] by replacing each coordinate factor
   $\Delta_0$ with $Q_0$ and each $\Delta_r$ ($r\ge1$) with
   $Q_r-Q_{r-1}$. Enumerate the resulting finite signed tensor rules in
   lexicographic multi-index order.
2. For each tensor rule, enumerate its finite node tuples in lexicographic
   coordinate-key order. Add its signed coefficient to a finite map indexed by
   the exact tuple key; initialize an unseen key with coefficient $0$.
3. Form $\mathcal N_\Lambda=\bigcup_{\ell\in\Lambda}
   X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}$, sort its distinct exact keys, and
   evaluate $f$ once at each of these keys. Return the map of combined
   coefficients and the finite sum of coefficient times function value. Set
   $W(\Lambda):=|\mathcal N_\Lambda|$, including any node whose combined
   coefficient is zero; this is the work convention used in this pair.

This is an exact-real finite procedure. Approximate floating-point node
comparisons, arithmetic, and function-evaluation error are outside its claims.

## Statement

Use the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy of
[[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]]. Let $d\ge1$. For
$S=\{j_1<\cdots<j_k\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, define
$$D_Sf:=\partial_{x_{j_k}}^4\cdots\partial_{x_{j_1}}^4f,$$
so these derivatives are applied in increasing coordinate order; set
$D_\varnothing f=f$. Assume every $D_Sf$ is continuous on the closed cube,
with the one-sided endpoint convention of
[[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]], and choose finite bounds $M_S\ge0$
such that $|D_Sf(x)|\le M_S$ on $[0,1]^d$. For
$\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d$, put $S(\ell):=\{j:\ell_j\ge1\}$ and
$$\delta_\ell(f):=(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Then
$$|\delta_\ell(f)|\le M_{S(\ell)}\left(\frac{17}{2880}\right)^{|S(\ell)|}16^{-\sum_{j\in S(\ell)}\ell_j}.$$
Moreover, for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$,
$$\sum_{\ell\in F}|\delta_\ell(f)|\le\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}M_S\left(\frac{17}{43200}\right)^{|S|}<\infty.$$

## Definition

**Input:** dimension $d\ge1$; a finite downward-closed cap
$\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ containing $0$; for each coordinate, the
one-dimensional quadrature rules from a hierarchy as in
[[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]] through every level used by
$\Gamma$, with canonical node keys that agree exactly if and only if the real
nodes agree and are totally ordered; a function $f$ evaluable at the nodes; and
an integer evaluation budget $B\ge0$. Admissible inputs supply all these rules
and keys at every level required by $\Gamma$.

**Output:** a current downward-closed index set $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$, its
Smolyak value when the initial rule fits the budget, the computed detail
surpluses, the distinct nodes actually sampled, and one status:
`budget-too-small`, `budget-exhausted`, or `frontier-exhausted`.

1. An index $\ell\in\Gamma\setminus\Lambda$ is **admissible** when every
   immediate predecessor $\ell-e_j$ with $\ell_j>0$ already belongs to
   $\Lambda$. Its **surplus** is the exact detail value $\delta_\ell(f)$ and
   its selection indicator is $|\delta_\ell(f)|$.
2. Form the baseline node set $X_0^d$. If its cardinality exceeds $B$, return
   `budget-too-small`, an empty $\Lambda$, no cubature value, and no sampled
   nodes. Otherwise set $\Lambda:=\{0\}$, initialize the active candidate set
   as empty, evaluate $f$ once at every baseline node, and set the current
   value to $Q_{\{0\}}(f)$. Then process every initially admissible index in
   $\Gamma\setminus\Lambda$ in lexicographic order using step 3.
3. Visit newly admissible indices in lexicographic order, skipping any index
   already recorded as active, accepted, or `uncomputed-budget`. To compute one
   surplus, form its finite tensor-detail node set and the new keys not already
   sampled. If adding them would exceed $B$, record this candidate as
   `uncomputed-budget` without evaluating those nodes. Otherwise evaluate each
   new key once, store the values, compute $\delta_\ell(f)$ from the finite
   signed weights, and add the index to the active candidate set.
4. If the active set is empty and an admissible `uncomputed-budget` candidate
   remains, return `budget-exhausted`. Otherwise, if the active set is empty,
   return `frontier-exhausted`.
5. Otherwise select the active index with largest absolute surplus, breaking
   ties lexicographically. Remove it from the active set, mark it accepted, add
   it to $\Lambda$, update the cubature value by adding its signed surplus, and
   inspect its finite forward neighbors for newly admissible indices; process
   them by step 3. Repeat from step 4.

The evaluation budget counts the union of distinct keys sampled while computing
both accepted and candidate surpluses. The indicator $|\delta_\ell(f)|$ is a
refinement heuristic only. A threshold on this indicator, or exhaustion of the
finite candidate cap, is not an error certificate unless a separate omitted-tail
bound applies.

$$|I_d(f)-Q_\Lambda(f)|\le\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d\setminus\Lambda}|\delta_\ell(f)|.$$

hypothesis for continuous $f$ by
[[lem-smolyak-dyadic-tensor-simpson-convergence]], and for the mixed-derivative

satisfies absolute summability.

[F2] [[def-smolyak-absolute-detail-summability]]: a nonnegative multi-index sum is the supremum of its finite subsums when these are bounded; the omitted tail uses the same definition on the complement of $\Lambda$.

[F4] [[lem-smolyak-dyadic-tensor-simpson-convergence]]: $Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)\to I_d(f)$.

[F5] [[lem-triangle-inequality-finite]]: the absolute value of each finite detail sum is at most the sum of its absolute terms.

[F6] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums split over disjoint finite index sets.

[F7] [[def-real-limit]]: convergence of a real sequence is tested using every positive rational tolerance.

[F8] [[lem-of-triangle-inequality]]: $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$ for real $x,y$.

[F9] [[lem-smolyak-mixed-simpson-detail-decay]]: under its continuous mixed fourth-derivative hypotheses, every finite absolute-detail subsum has the common finite bound $\sum_{S\subseteq[d]}M_S(17/43200)^{|S|}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $d\ge1$, $n\ge2d$, and $f$ with the continuous mixed derivatives and finite bounds in [[lem-smolyak-mixed-simpson-detail-decay]].

[F6] [[cor-compositions-with-k-parts-are-counted-by-binomial-coefficients]]: compositions of $m$ into $k$ positive parts are counted by $\binom{m-1}{k-1}$ for $m,k\ge1$.

[F8] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is strictly increasing on positive reals, $\log1=0$, $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$, and repeated use gives $\log(2^n)=n\log2$; in particular $\log2>0$.

[F12] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: every nonempty real set bounded above has a finite supremum.

[F13] [[lem-power-monotone]] and [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]: if $r\ge1$ and $j\ge1$, then $r^j\ge r>0$, so $r^{-j}\le r^{-1}$ (with equality when $r^j=r$, and reciprocal order when $r^j>r$); powers are as in [[def-integer-power]].

A node tuple belongs to $\mathcal N_{\Lambda_n}$ iff its minimal-level vector $t$ satisfies $|t|_1\le n$: that condition itself supplies an admissible index, and any index containing the tuple has each coordinate at least its minimal level. ## Definition

**Inputs:** $T>0$, $d\ge1$, $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, a state $y\in U\subseteq\mathbb C^d$, a step $(t,h)$ with $0\le t<t+h\le T$, a method choice $E$ or $2$, a field $g:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb C^d$, a nonnegative state-Lipschitz bound $L$ on an admitted tube containing the input and, when method $2$ is selected, the exact and computed ETD2 predictor stages, a certified semigroup bound $\|e^{sA}\|_2\le M e^{\omega s}$ for $0\le s\le h$ with $M\ge1$ and $\omega\in\mathbb R$, finite Arnoldi budgets $1\le m_0\le d$, $1\le m_1\le d+1$, $1\le m_2\le d+2$, certified field-evaluation, membership, scalar-enclosure, and vector-arithmetic providers, and a finite integer cap $C_{\max}\ge0$ for all nested backend/provider calls in this step. Each service call must terminate for the supplied finite budgets, supply a finite pre-call upper bound for its total nested call count, and return its actual call count and work counters. The step is admissible only when the initial state and every evaluated stage have certified membership in $U$ and, for method $2$, the exact ETD2 predictor also has certified membership in $U$; every needed service-call bound must fit within the remaining $C_{\max}$.

For each nonzero Arnoldi action request with matrix $B$, positive time $\tau$, and input $u$, the backend must certify a relation $BV_j=V_jH_j+\gamma v_{j+1}e_j^*+D+\Omega$ with $\beta,\gamma,\eta_i,\eta_{\rm orth},\eta_{\rm init},\nu_V,\epsilon_{\rm red},\eta_{\rm proj}\ge0$, $\|v_{j+1}\|_2=1$ when $\gamma>0$, $\|d_i\|_2\le\eta_i$, $\|\Omega\|_2\le\eta_{\rm orth}$, $\|u-\beta V_je_1\|_2\le\eta_{\rm init}$, $\|V_j\|_2\le\nu_V$, $\mu_2(B)\le\rho_B$ with $\rho_B\ge0$, and $\|H_j\|_2\le\rho_H$ with $\rho_H\ge0$. Its reduced-action certificate $\epsilon_{\rm red}$ may be used only when the reduced scaled-Taylor call has `success`: [[thm-scaled-taylor-exponential-action-error-and-work]] then bounds that call's error, and any subsequent scaling error is included. The backend also returns a final-projection error $\eta_{\rm proj}$, an actual work record, and its total nested-call count. Missing or uncertified bounds, work counters, or call counts make that request inconclusive. In exact Arnoldi, the exact relation, initial representation, and orthonormal basis supply the corresponding relation bounds.

For each positive-time request, compute the full action-error bound from [[thm-arnoldi-exponential-action-error-bound]] using
$$\epsilon_{\rm act}:=e^{\rho_B\tau}\eta_{\rm init}+\beta\tau e^{\tau\max(\rho_B,\rho_H)}\left(\gamma+\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^j\eta_i^2}+\eta_{\rm orth}\right)+\nu_V\epsilon_{\rm red}+\eta_{\rm proj}.$$
If any required quantity or its upward-rounded arithmetic enclosure is missing, return inconclusive. Define an action request $\operatorname{Act}(k,v)$ for $k=0,1,2$ as follows. If $v=0$, return the exact zero vector with bound zero and zero action work before constructing any augmented matrix. For $k=0$ and $v\ne0$, call [[alg-arnoldi-exponential-and-phi-actions]] with matrix $A$, time $h$, input $v$, index $0$, and budget $m_0$. For $k=1,2$ and $v\ne0$, use [[thm-phi-recurrence-and-augmented-matrix-actions]]: let $J_k$ have ones on its superdiagonal, let $e_1,e_k$ be the first and last coordinate vectors in $\mathbb C^k$, set

and call [[alg-arnoldi-exponential-and-phi-actions]] with matrix $B_k(hA,v)$, time $1$, input $w_k$, index $0$, and budget $m_k$. Here $w_k\ne0$; the zero-phi-input shortcut was applied to $v$ before forming this augmented request. By [[thm-phi-recurrence-and-augmented-matrix-actions]], the top $d$ coordinates of $e^{B_k(hA,v)}w_k$ equal $\varphi_k(hA)v$. In either nonzero case compute the full action-error bound using its certified Arnoldi relation and successful reduced-action certificate, then project to the requested vector; coordinate projection cannot increase the Euclidean error. Here $\varphi_0(hA)=e^{hA}$.

The calling implementation instruments each [[alg-arnoldi-exponential-and-phi-actions]] request and its nested providers, then returns the actual work counters and total nested-call count with that action result. The work record is $W=(N_A,N_{\rm other},W_{\rm dense})$: $N_A$ counts actual products with $A$, including the upper-left $hA$ multiplication inside each augmented $B_k$ product; $N_{\rm other}$ counts products with every other matrix, including augmented and reduced matrices and final projection matrices; $W_{\rm dense}$ records the backend's declared matrix-function work for dense implementations. 1. Initialize all work counters and $C$ to zero. If any needed membership check or service-call upper bound cannot be certified, or the global call budget cannot fit a required service call, return `inconclusive`. A failed provider response with no sound bound is `inconclusive`.
2. Evaluate $g(t,y)$ as $\widetilde q_0$ with a certified error $\eta_0$, reserving its pre-call upper count first and then adding its actual count to $C$. Request $\operatorname{Act}(0,y)$ and $\operatorname{Act}(1,\widetilde q_0)$, reserving and accumulating their call/work counters. A zero phi input is handled by $\operatorname{Act}$ before any Arnoldi call. If a request is inconclusive, return inconclusive without accepting a step. Denote the candidates by $\widehat E y$ and $\widehat P_1$ and their bounds by $\epsilon_0,\epsilon_1$.
3. For method $E$, form $\widetilde y^+=\widehat E y+h\widehat P_1$. If $\alpha_E$ bounds the scalar/vector arithmetic error in this combination and its provider call fits the remaining call cap, accumulate its counters and set
$$\delta_n=\epsilon_0+h(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0)+\alpha_E.$$
4. For method $2$, first form the predictor candidate $\widetilde a=\widehat E y+h\widehat P_1$ using a certified arithmetic provider and accumulate its work/call counters. Check $(t+h,\widetilde a)$ for certified membership in the domain and admitted tube before evaluating $g(t+h,\widetilde a)$. A certified-false membership result returns `invalid-input`; an inconclusive membership result returns `inconclusive`. If $\alpha_a$ bounds the predictor arithmetic error, set $\eta_a:=\epsilon_0+h(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0)+\alpha_a$. Evaluate $g(t+h,\widetilde a)$ as $\widetilde q_a$ with a certified error $\eta_a^g$, reserving and accumulating its service counters. Request $\operatorname{Act}(2,\widetilde q_0)$ and $\operatorname{Act}(2,\widetilde q_a)$; if either request is inconclusive, return inconclusive without accepting a step. With their action-error bounds $\epsilon_{20},\epsilon_{2a}$, form
$$\widetilde y^+=\widehat E y+h(\widehat P_1-\widehat P_{20}+\widehat P_{2a}),$$
where $\widehat P_{20}$ and $\widehat P_{2a}$ are the two $\varphi_2$ candidates. If $\alpha_2$ bounds the final combination arithmetic error and its provider call fits the remaining call cap, accumulate its counters and set
$$\delta_n=\epsilon_0+h\left(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0+\epsilon_{20}+\frac{B_h}{2}\eta_0+\epsilon_{2a}+\frac{B_h}{2}(L\eta_a+\eta_a^g)\right)+\alpha_2.$$
5. Before returning `certified`, verify all action calls have certified Arnoldi relations, reduced-action status `success`, and certified final projections; all field-evaluation and arithmetic bounds are finite; all returned work/call counters are present and within their pre-call bounds; and the displayed scalar calculations have certified upward enclosures. If any check fails, return `inconclusive` and do not accept the step. Return the accrued work record and $C$ with every status.

Every scalar bound computation, including $\epsilon_{\rm act}$, $B_h$, and $\delta_n$, is rounded upward with a certified enclosure; if its enclosure is missing or fails to dominate the exact expression, return inconclusive. The returned work record is the sum of the actual counts supplied by the services for the action requests and arithmetic/evaluation operations. The finite call cap and each finite nested-action budget are checked before calls; the exact mathematical map is not a zero-cost oracle.

## Statement

Let $T>0$, $N\ge1$, $h=T/N$, $t_n=nh$, $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, and let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb C^d$ be open after realification, with $g:D\to\mathbb C^d$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb C^d$ solve
$$y'(t)=Ay(t)+g(t,y(t))$$
Suppose the exact path, every numerical state, and every ETD2 predictor lie in a common compact time-state tube $\mathcal T\subset D$ with positive margin. Also assume the hypotheses of [[lem-exponential-integrator-interaction-picture-stability]] hold on this tube: compared inputs in each time fiber and both associated ETD2 predictor states are admissible, and $g$ is $L_g$-Lipschitz between the states and stages used there. Finally, let $q(t):=g(t,y(t))$ be $C^2$ with $\|q'\|_2\le Q_1$ and $\|q''\|_2\le Q_2$. Assume
$$\|e^{sA}\|_2\le M e^{\omega s}\quad(0\le s\le T),\qquad M\ge1,\quad \omega\in\mathbb R,$$
and put
$$K_+:=\sup_{0\le s\le T}\|e^{sA}\|_2,\quad K_-:=\sup_{0\le s\le T}\|e^{-sA}\|_2,\quad \kappa:=L_gK_+K_-.$$
These finite-matrix suprema are finite; in particular $K_+\le M e^{\max(\omega,0)T}$. Define
$$C_E:=\frac{K_+Q_1}{2},\quad C_2:=K_+\left(Q_2+\frac{L_gC_E}{2}\right),\quad L_E:=\kappa,\quad L_2:=\kappa+\frac{T\kappa^2}{2}.$$
For an exact-action exponential-Euler run use $p=1,C_p=C_E,L_p=L_E$; for exact-action ETD2 use $p=2,C_p=C_2,L_p=L_2$. If $\Gamma(L,T):=(e^{LT}-1)/L$ for $L>0$ and $\Gamma(0,T):=T$, then exact initial data give
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le K_+K_-C_p\Gamma(L_p,T)h^p.$$

Now let a certified-action implementation return candidates $\widetilde y_{n+1}$ and certified one-step action-error bounds $\delta_n$ as in [[lem-certified-exponential-step-action-error]]. Starting from $\widetilde y_0=y(0)$, its error obeys
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|\widetilde y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le K_+K_-e^{L_pT}\left(C_pT h^p+\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\delta_j\right).$$
Thus local orders one and two imply fixed-$A$, finite-dimensional global orders one and two when exact actions are used or when $\sum_j\delta_j=O(h^p)$. The constants may depend on $A$, $T$, the tube, and the derivative bounds. The bounds are not asserted uniformly over varying matrices or growing dimensions; no unbounded-operator/PDE convergence theorem follows without the additional domain and commutator hypotheses such a theorem requires.

## Definition

Let $M,d\ge1$, let $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$ be distinct collocation nodes, and let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_M$ be their cardinal polynomials from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
$$Q_{ij}:=\int_0^{c_i}\ell_j(s)\,ds,\qquad b_j:=\int_0^1\ell_j(s)\,ds.$$
The matrix $Q\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ and vector $b\in\mathbb R^M$ are the collocation tableau coefficients. For an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$ on the open domain of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], write
$$F_j(U):=f(t+c_jh,U_j),\qquad QF(U):=\left(\sum_{j=1}^M Q_{ij}F_j(U)\right)_{i=1}^M.$$
All displayed integrals use the oriented Riemann convention of [[def-oriented-integral]]. In particular $Q_{ij}=0$ when $c_i=0$, and the integral in $u_h$ vanishes at $\tau=0$. The collocation stages and endpoint are the implicit Runge–Kutta equations of [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] with $A=Q$, nodes $c$, and weights $b$:
$$U=\mathbf1u+hQF(U),\qquad \Psi_h(t,u)=u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U).$$
The associated collocation polynomial on normalized time $\tau\in[0,1]$ is
$$u_h(\tau):=u+h\int_0^\tau\sum_{j=1}^M\ell_j(s)F_j(U)\,ds.$$
Thus $u_h(c_i)=U_i$, $u_h'(c_i)=hF_i(U)$, and $u_h(1)=\Psi_h(t,u)$ whenever $U$ is an admissible solution. This definition alone asserts no branch existence or uniqueness.

For interpolation estimates define the **Lebesgue constant** of this fixed node set by
$$\Lambda_M:=\max_{0\le s\le1}\sum_{j=1}^M|\ell_j(s)|.$$
For a real matrix $A$, write $\|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|$. These constants depend on the nodes and on $M$; no uniform-in-$M$ bound is part of the definition.

## Definition

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be the open time-state domain of an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$, with $d\ge1$. The inputs are a time $t\in\mathbb R$, an initial state $u\in\mathbb R^d$ with $(t,u)\in D$, a step $h>0$, an integer $M\ge1$, distinct ordered nodes $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$, a predictor (default $U^0=\mathbf1u$), a Lipschitz bound $L\ge0$, a tolerance $\mathrm{tol}>0$, an integer sweep budget $K\ge0$, and a supplied stage set $\mathcal C$. A stage vector $U$ is admissible only when $(t+c_jh,U_j)\in D$ for every $j$.

After validating the node data, form the collocation tableau $Q,b$ of [[def-collocation-quadrature-tableau]]. Let $c_0=0$, $\Delta c_j=c_j-c_{j-1}$, and define the left-Euler node-subinterval preconditioner by its initial column $a_i=c_1$ and stage block
$$ (Q_\Delta)_{ij}=\begin{cases}\Delta c_{j+1},&j<i,\\0,&j\ge i.\end{cases} $$
The stage block is strictly lower triangular. In augmented notation, set $\widehat Q=(0\mid Q)$, $\widehat Q_\Delta=(a\mid Q_\Delta)$, and $\widehat F(U)=(f(t,u),F(U))$. One sweep is
$$U^{k+1}=\mathbf1u+h\widehat Q_\Delta\widehat F(U^{k+1})+h(\widehat Q-\widehat Q_\Delta)\widehat F(U^k).$$
The fixed initial-column contributions cancel, so the procedure below does not evaluate $F_0=f(t,u)$. For a stage vector $U$, write $F_j(U)=f(t+c_jh,U_j)$. Since $Q_\Delta$ is strictly lower triangular, for fixed previous stages $U^k$ the unique new stages are computed in increasing $i$ by the forward recursion
$$U_i^{k+1}=u+h\sum_{j<i}(Q_\Delta)_{ij}F_j(U^{k+1})+h\sum_{j=1}^M(Q_{ij}-(Q_\Delta)_{ij})F_j(U^k),\quad i=1,\ldots,M.$$

Use $\|V\|_{\infty,2}=\max_i\|V_i\|_2$ and $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|$. The supplied set $\mathcal C$ must be a nonempty closed product ball of admissible stage vectors, contain the predictor, be invariant under each inner stage map and outer sweep, and have an $L$-Lipschitz stage field $F(U)=(F_j(U))_{j=1}^M$ in this norm. After forming $Q_\Delta$, compute $a=hL\|Q_\Delta\|_\infty$. If $a\ge1$, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. For $a<1$, compute $q=hL\|Q-Q_\Delta\|_\infty/(1-a)$; if $q\ge1$ or invariance is not certified, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. The exact procedure is:

1. Reject repeated, unordered, or out-of-range nodes as `invalid-node-data` before forming the tableau.
2. Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ from the valid nodes and apply the contraction and invariance checks described above.
3. If the predictor is outside $\mathcal C$ or any required stage evaluation $(t+c_jh,U_j)$ lies outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint.
4. Evaluate and store all $M$ values $F_j(U^0)$ once.
5. If $K=0$, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; no residual test has been performed.
6. For $k=0,1,\ldots,K-1$, compute $U^{k+1}$ in increasing stage order using the displayed recursion, reusing the stored $F(U^k)$ and evaluating each new $F_j(U^{k+1})$ once. If a new stage is outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint. Then compute $r_k=\|U^{k+1}-U^k\|_{\infty,2}$. If $r_k\le(1-q)\,\mathrm{tol}$, return status `residual-tolerance-met`, the stage vector $U^k$, and endpoint $u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U^k)$. If this is the $K$th sweep and the test failed, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; otherwise use $U^{k+1}$ and its stored field values as the next iterate.

These statuses report only the stated branch outcome; they do not assert convergence when a check fails.

Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ once per invocation and retain their coefficients through the sweep loop. Retain the old and current stage vectors and their field values while computing a sweep and testing its residual. On continuation, reuse these buffers for the next sweep; on acceptance, use the retained $U^k$ and $F(U^k)$ for the returned stage vector and endpoint in step 6. Perform the displayed operations in exact real arithmetic.

## Definition

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $N\ge1$, and for $0\le n\le N$ let $U_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_n}$ be open. A finite parameterized state-step graph consists of a $C^1$ initial map $x_0:\Theta\to U_0$ and $C^1$ step maps $\Psi_n:U_n\times\Theta\to U_{n+1}$ for $0\le n<N$, such that the recursion $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$ is defined for every $\theta$ in the chosen parameter neighborhood. A $C^1$ running objective consists of maps $\ell_n:U_n\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and a terminal objective $\phi:U_N\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, all $C^1$. Its reduced objective is
$$J(\theta)=\phi(x_N(\theta),\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\ell_n(x_n(\theta),\theta).$$
The maps and objective define one finite real-arithmetic graph. A gradient of this graph is the derivative of this finite composition; it is not the derivative of an exact implicit solution unless the step map itself is that solution map.

## Definition

Let $V$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and write $V^*$ for the continuous real dual. A parameter-dependent coercive elliptic variational problem is a family of bounded bilinear forms $a_\theta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ and bounded linear functionals $\ell_\theta\in V^*$ such that, on each parameter neighborhood under discussion, $\|a_\theta\|\le M$ and $a_\theta(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$ for fixed $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$. Operator-norm $C^1$ data means that the maps $\theta\mapsto A_\theta\in\mathcal L(V,V^*)$, $A_\theta u:=a_\theta(u,\cdot)$, and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta\in V^*$ are continuously Fréchet differentiable. A state at $\theta$ is a vector $u_\theta\in V$ satisfying $a_\theta(u_\theta,v)=\ell_\theta(v)$ for every $v\in V$. When a state is specified, a $C^1$ objective $J:V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ defines the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$. This definition alone asserts neither state existence nor uniqueness of an optimizer.

Define $p_N=D_x\phi(x_N,\theta)^T$ and, backward for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$,
$$p_n=D_x\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+A_n^Tp_{n+1}.$$
The exact gradient of the finite objective is
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(x_N,\theta)^T+S_0^Tp_0+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(D_\theta\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}\bigr).$$

**Given:** The open finite state-step graph, its $C^1$ maps, objective, trajectory and parameter in the Statement.

1.2 Apply the reverse accumulation rule [F2] to the finite graph of states and objective summands in [F1]. The terminal contribution seeds $p_N=D_x\phi^T$; at each state node $x_n$, its local running-cost edge contributes $D_x\ell_n^T$, while its state-transition edge contributes $A_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Thus the accumulated state cotangent is exactly $p_n$ as defined in the Statement, and the direct parameter edges contribute $D_\theta\phi^T$ and $D_\theta\ell_n^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. ## Statement

$$A_kQ_{k-1}=Q_kR_k,$$
where $Q_k$ is orthogonal and $R_k$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal $r_{k,ii}$. Put $P_N=A_N\cdots A_1$ and define the exact finite-time log-volume change by $\log|\det P_N|$. Then
$$\log|\det P_N|=\sum_{k=1}^N\sum_{i=1}^n\log r_{k,ii}.$$
No infinite-time Lyapunov exponent or shadowing conclusion follows.

For a numerical log record, define $\sigma_{\min}(A):=\inf_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Ax\|_2$. If $\sigma_{\min}(A_k)\ge\sigma>0$, each exact $r_{k,ii}\ge\sigma$. If positive computed diagonals $\widetilde r_{k,ii}$ satisfy $|\widetilde r_{k,ii}-r_{k,ii}|\le\varepsilon_{k,i}\le\sigma/2$, and each computed logarithm $\widehat l_{k,i}$ satisfies $|\widehat l_{k,i}-\log\widetilde r_{k,ii}|\le\delta_{k,i}$, then
$$\left|\sum_{k,i}\widehat l_{k,i}-\log|\det P_N|\right|\le\sum_{k,i}\left(\frac{2\varepsilon_{k,i}}{\sigma}+\delta_{k,i}\right).$$

## Statement

Let $s\ge1$, let $R_1,\ldots,R_s$ be complex matrices of one fixed shape,
and let $C\ge1$. Define
$$\mathcal C_{s,C}:=\{c\in\mathbb R^s:\sum_{i=1}^s c_i=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^s|c_i|\le C\}$$
and $J(c):=\|\sum_{i=1}^s c_iR_i\|_F^2$. Then $J$ attains a minimum on
$\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Among all minimizers there is a unique vector of minimum
Euclidean norm. This rule defines the exact capped DIIS coefficient vector even
when the least-squares Gram matrix is singular.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A positive integer $s$, matrices $R_i$ of the same finite shape, and a real cap $C\ge1$.

[F1] The Frobenius norm is a norm on the finite-dimensional matrix space ([[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]).

[F2] A closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^s$ is compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and a continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its minimum ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F3] Real absolute values satisfy $|a+b|\le|a|+|b|$ and $|ab|=|a||b|$ ([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]).

## Proof


1.1 The vector $e_1=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ belongs to $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ because its entries sum to $1$ and its $\ell^1$ norm is $1\le C$. Thus the coefficient set is nonempty. It is closed: the sum constraint is the inverse image of the closed singleton $\{1\}$ under a continuous linear map, and the $\ell^1$ bound is the inverse image of the closed interval $(-\infty,C]$ under the continuous function $c\mapsto\sum_i|c_i|$. It is bounded because $\|c\|_1^2=\sum_i c_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}|c_i||c_j|\ge\|c\|_2^2$ and $\|c\|_1\le C$. Therefore [F2] makes $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ compact. [given, F2]

2.1 The map $c\mapsto\sum_i c_iR_i$ is linear and continuous in finite dimensions, and its squared Frobenius norm is continuous by [F1]. The extreme-value theorem gives a minimum; its minimizer set is closed as the inverse image of the singleton containing that minimum, hence compact as a closed subset of $\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Thus [F2] gives a nonempty compact set $M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in\mathcal C_{s,C}}J(c)$. [step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 For $c,d\in\mathcal C_{s,C}$ and $0\le t\le1$, the coefficients $e=(1-t)c+td$ satisfy $\sum_i e_i=(1-t)\sum_i c_i+t\sum_i d_i=1$. By [F3], $\sum_i|e_i|\le(1-t)\sum_i|c_i|+t\sum_i|d_i|\le C$, so $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ is convex. The set $M$ is also convex: for matrices $A,B$ the identity $\|(1-t)A+tB\|_F^2=(1-t)\|A\|_F^2+t\|B\|_F^2-t(1-t)\|A-B\|_F^2$ proves convexity of the squared norm. Applying it to $A=\sum_i c_iR_i$ and $B=\sum_i d_iR_i$ shows $J((1-t)c+td)\le(1-t)J(c)+tJ(d)=\min J$, so the convex combination also minimizes. Since $M$ is compact, the continuous function $c\mapsto\|c\|_2^2$ has a minimizer $c_*\in M$. [step 2.1, F1, F3, algebra]

4.1 If distinct $c,d\in M$ both had minimum Euclidean norm, their midpoint would lie in $M$ and satisfy $\left\|\frac{c+d}{2}\right\|_2^2=\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2}-\frac{\|c-d\|_2^2}{4}<\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2},$ contradicting minimality. Thus $c_*$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares minimizer. No nonsingularity of the Gram matrix is needed for existence or tie-breaking. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, with square-summability as in [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Define the diagonal operator $A$ by
$$D(A)=\left\{u\in\mathcal H:\sum_{k\ge1} k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad (Au)_k=-k^2u_k.$$
Let $g\in\mathcal H$ be the fixed sequence $g_k=1/k$ for odd $k$ and $g_k=0$ for even $k$; membership follows from [[thm-p-series-real-exponents]] with exponent $2$. The split evolution is $u'=Au+g$. For $t\ge0$, define the exact diagonal subflow $E_tu=(e^{-k^2t}u_k)_{k\ge1}$ and the exact translation subflow $B_tu=u+tg$. By [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $0<e^{-k^2t}\le1$, so each $E_t$ maps $\mathcal H$ to itself; each $B_t$ does so because $g\in\mathcal H$. The associated Strang modal step is
$$S_h=E_{h/2}\circ B_h\circ E_{h/2},\qquad h>0,$$
where the rightmost map is applied first. Each coordinate of $E_t$ solves $u_k'=-k^2u_k$, and each coordinate of $B_t$ solves $u_k'=g_k$. This is a precisely defined sequence-space model; it records one Dirichlet sine-mode boundary mismatch and makes no general convergence assertion for unbounded PDE operators.

## Statement

Let $\mathcal H$, $A$, and $E_t$ be as in [[def-dirichlet-sine-mode-heat-splitting-model]]. The maps $E_t$ for $t\ge0$ satisfy $E_0=I$ and $E_{t+s}=E_tE_s$, are contractions in $\ell^2$, and are strongly continuous at $t=0$. Define the generator domain to consist of those $u\in\mathcal H$ for which the right limit
$$\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{E_tu-u}{t}$$
exists in $\mathcal H$. This domain is exactly $D(A)=\{u:\sum_{k\ge1}k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\}$, and the limit equals $Au=(-k^2u_k)_{k\ge1}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The sequence space, diagonal operator, and maps in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-dirichlet-sine-mode-heat-splitting-model]] and [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]: $u\in\mathcal H$ means $\sum_{k\ge1}|u_k|^2<\infty$, and $(E_tu)_k=e^{-k^2t}u_k$.

[F2] [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]: $e^{x+y}=e^xe^y$ and $e^0=1$.

[F3] [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]: $e^x>0$, and $x\le y$ implies $e^x\le e^y$.

[F4] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: the scalar exponential is differentiable with derivative $e^x$, its compositions obey the chain rule, and a differentiable scalar function on an interval obeys the mean-value theorem.

## Proof

1.1 Coordinatewise, [F2] gives $e^{-k^2(t+s)}=e^{-k^2t}e^{-k^2s}$ and $E_0u=u$, so $E_{t+s}=E_tE_s$. If $t\ge0$, [F3] gives $0<e^{-k^2t}\le1$; hence $\sum_k|(E_tu)_k|^2\le\sum_k|u_k|^2$, proving that $E_t$ maps $\mathcal H$ to itself and is a contraction. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 For every $x\ge0$, [F4] applied to $s\mapsto e^{-s}$ on $[0,x]$ gives $0\le1-e^{-x}\le x$: the difference is $xe^{-\xi}$ for some $\xi\in[0,x]$, and [F3] bounds $e^{-\xi}$ by $1$. For $u\in D(A)$, the $k$th coordinate of $(E_tu-u)/t$ tends to $-k^2u_k$ by the chain rule and exponential derivative in [F4]. Its difference from that limit has absolute value at most $2k^2|u_k|$, by the same bound. The squared tail of these differences is therefore at most $4\sum_{k>K}k^4|u_k|^2$, which tends to zero; on every finite head the coordinate limits give norm convergence. Hence the right limit exists in $\mathcal H$ and equals $Au$. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Fix $u\in\mathcal H$ and $\varepsilon>0$. By convergence of its square sum, choose $K$ so that $\sum_{k>K}|u_k|^2<\varepsilon^2/4$. The squared norm of the tail of $E_tu-u$ is at most this tail because $|e^{-k^2t}-1|\le1$ by [F3]; for the finitely many indices $k\le K$, continuity of the exponential at zero from [F4] makes their squared sum less than $\varepsilon^2/4$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$. Thus $\|E_tu-u\|_2<\varepsilon$, proving strong continuity at zero. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra, choose]

3.1 Conversely, suppose $(E_tu-u)/t$ converges in $\mathcal H$ to $v$. For each $k$, coordinate evaluation is continuous since $|w_k|\le\|w\|_2$; therefore its limit is $v_k=-k^2u_k$, using [F4]. Since $v\in\mathcal H$, $\sum_k k^4|u_k|^2=\sum_k|v_k|^2<\infty$, so $u\in D(A)$. Together with step 1.2 this identifies the generator domain and its value. [F1, F4, step 1.2, algebra] ∎
